subject: biology
title: Unit 1 summary and memory tips
summary: A condensed revision sheet for all of Unit 1: cells, organelles, membrane transport, the cell cycle, stem cells, plant and animal systems, homeostasis and its failures, and investigation skills, plus memory tips.
body:
This revision sheet squeezes the whole of Unit 1 (How do organisms regulate their functions?) into one place. Use it after you have worked through the individual lessons: read a section, cover it, and try to say the key points out loud before checking. The memory tips at the end collect the best tricks for making the facts stick.

## Area of Study 1: How do cells function?

### Cell theory and cell types

- **Cell theory** has three ideas: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.
- Every cell has a **plasma membrane**, **cytosol**, **ribosomes** and **DNA**.
- **Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their circular chromosome sits in the **nucleoid**, and they often carry small circular **plasmids**. They are small (roughly 1–10 µm).
- **Eukaryotic cells** (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and are usually 10–100 µm.
- Plant cells have a cellulose **cell wall**, **chloroplasts** and a large central **vacuole**; animal cells do not. Cell walls are made of cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi and peptidoglycan in bacteria.

| Feature | Prokaryote | Eukaryote |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | No (nucleoid) | Yes |
| Membrane-bound organelles | No | Yes |
| Ribosomes | Yes (smaller) | Yes |
| DNA | Circular, plus plasmids | Linear chromosomes in nucleus |
| Typical size | 1–10 µm | 10–100 µm |

### Surface area to volume ratio

- **SA:V** = surface area ÷ volume. For a cube of side length s: SA = 6s², V = s³, so SA:V = 6 ÷ s.
- As a cell gets bigger, volume grows faster than surface area, so SA:V falls. The membrane can no longer exchange materials fast enough for the cell's needs. This limits cell size.
- Cells raise SA:V by staying small, being flat or thin, or folding their membrane (for example **microvilli** on intestinal cells).

### Organelles and compartmentalisation

- **Compartmentalisation**: membranes divide the eukaryotic cell into separate spaces so different reactions can happen at once without interfering.
- **Nucleus**: double membrane; stores DNA.
- **Ribosomes**: RNA and protein, no membrane; make proteins.
- **Rough ER**: studded with ribosomes; folds and transports proteins.
- **Smooth ER**: no ribosomes; makes lipids and breaks down some toxins.
- **Golgi apparatus**: modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles.
- **Mitochondria**: double membrane; site of most of cellular respiration (ATP production).
- **Chloroplasts**: double membrane; site of photosynthesis.
- **Lysosomes**: vesicles of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out parts and engulfed material.
- **Vesicles**: small membrane sacs that carry substances around the cell.
- **Cytoskeleton**: protein fibres that give shape and move things within the cell.
- The protein export pathway: ribosome → rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane (exocytosis).
- Structure matches function: secretory cells have lots of rough ER and Golgi; very active cells (muscle, sperm) have many mitochondria.

### The plasma membrane and transport

- The **fluid mosaic model**: a fluid **phospholipid bilayer** (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in) with proteins, cholesterol and carbohydrate chains scattered through it. The membrane is **selectively permeable**.
- Small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass straight through the bilayer. Ions and large polar molecules (Na⁺, glucose) need protein channels or carriers.

| Process | Direction | Needs protein? | Needs ATP? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple diffusion | Down gradient | No | No |
| Facilitated diffusion | Down gradient | Yes (channel or carrier) | No |
| Osmosis | Water towards higher solute concentration | Often through aquaporins | No |
| Active transport | Against gradient | Yes (carrier pump) | Yes |
| Endocytosis / exocytosis | Bulk in / out in vesicles | No | Yes |

- **Hypotonic** solution: lower solute concentration than the cell, so water enters. Animal cells swell and may burst; plant cells become **turgid**.
- **Hypertonic** solution: higher solute concentration, so water leaves. Animal cells shrivel; plant cells undergo **plasmolysis** (membrane pulls away from the wall).
- **Isotonic**: no net water movement.

### The cell cycle

- **Binary fission** (prokaryotes): copy the circular chromosome, move the copies apart as the cell lengthens, then split into two identical cells.
- The eukaryotic **cell cycle**: **interphase** (G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 growth and preparation) then M phase (**mitosis** and **cytokinesis**).
- Mitosis stages: **prophase** (chromosomes condense, spindle forms, nuclear membrane breaks down), **metaphase** (chromosomes line up across the middle), **anaphase** (**sister chromatids** pulled to opposite poles by **spindle fibres**), **telophase** (nuclear membranes re-form).
- Mitosis makes two genetically identical nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent (46 in a human body cell).
- Cytokinesis: animal cells pinch in (cleavage furrow); plant cells build a cell plate.
- **Checkpoints** at G1, G2 and M check cell size, DNA damage, complete replication and chromosome attachment before the cycle continues.

### Apoptosis and cancer

- **Apoptosis** is programmed, orderly cell death: the cell shrinks and breaks into membrane-wrapped fragments that phagocytes eat, so there is no inflammation. It shapes development (for example, removing webbing between fingers) and removes damaged cells.
- It can be triggered from inside the cell (the **intrinsic** or mitochondrial pathway, after DNA damage) or from outside (the **extrinsic** pathway, when a signal binds a death receptor). Both activate **caspase** enzymes that dismantle the cell.
- **Cancer** is uncontrolled cell division caused by mutations. Mutated **proto-oncogenes** become **oncogenes** that push division (the accelerator stuck on); mutated **tumour suppressor genes** stop slowing division or triggering apoptosis (the brakes fail).
- A tumour that spreads to other parts of the body has undergone **metastasis**.

### Stem cells

- A **stem cell** can self-renew and **differentiate** into specialised cells. Differentiation switches different genes on and off; the DNA itself does not change.
- **Potency** ladder: **totipotent** (zygote; all cells including the placenta) → **pluripotent** (inner cell mass of the **blastocyst**; any body cell) → **multipotent** (for example bone marrow stem cells; a related group of cells) → **unipotent** (one cell type).
- **Embryonic stem cells**: pluripotent, but destroying embryos raises ethical issues and the cells may be rejected.
- **Adult stem cells**: fewer ethical issues and can be patient-matched, but only multipotent.
- **Induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells**: body cells reprogrammed to be pluripotent; patient-matched, but there are concerns about safety (for example tumour formation).
- Bone marrow transplants are an established stem cell therapy; many others are still being researched.

## Area of Study 2: How do plant and animal systems function?

### Levels of organisation

`cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism`

- **Cell specialisation**: cells develop structures suited to a particular job.
- A **tissue** is a group of similar cells doing one job; an **organ** is several tissues working together; an **organ system** is several organs working together.

### Plant systems: water and nutrient transport

- **Root hairs** give a huge surface area. Mineral ions enter by active transport; water follows by osmosis.
- **Xylem**: dead, hollow, lignified tubes carrying water and minerals upward only.
- **Phloem**: living **sieve tube** elements with **companion cells** (which supply ATP), carrying sugars from **source** (for example a mature leaf) to **sink** (roots, fruit, growing tips). This movement is **translocation** and needs ATP for loading.
- **Transpiration**: water vapour evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through **stomata**.
- **Cohesion–tension model**: transpiration pulls on a continuous water column; **cohesion** (water molecules sticking to each other by hydrogen bonds) keeps the column together, and **adhesion** (water sticking to xylem walls) helps it climb. No ATP is needed.
- **Guard cells** open stomata when turgid and close them when flaccid. Stomata are a trade-off: open lets CO₂ in for photosynthesis but lets water out.
- Transpiration is faster when it is hot, dry (low humidity), windy and bright.

### Animal systems

- **Digestive system**: **mechanical digestion** (chewing, churning) and **chemical digestion** (enzymes). **Peristalsis** moves food along. The small intestine absorbs nutrients across **villi** and **microvilli**, which increase surface area. Bile from the liver **emulsifies** fats.
- **Endocrine system**: glands secrete **hormones** into the blood; only **target cells** with matching receptors respond. Slower and longer-lasting than nervous signals.
- **Excretory system**: the liver **deaminates** excess amino acids, making ammonia, then urea. The kidneys remove urea. In each **nephron**: filtration at the **glomerulus** into Bowman's capsule, selective reabsorption of useful substances (all glucose, most water and salts) back into the blood, and secretion of some wastes into the tubule.
- Systems link up through the blood: absorbed amino acids → liver makes urea → kidneys excrete it; the pancreas makes both digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.

### Homeostasis

- **Homeostasis**: keeping the internal environment (blood plasma and tissue fluid) within a tolerance range around a **set point**.
- The **stimulus–response model**: `stimulus → receptor → control centre (modulator) → effector → response`
- **Negative feedback**: the response reverses the original change, then switches off once the variable is back in range.
- **Temperature** (control centre: hypothalamus). Too hot: **vasodilation** and sweating. Too cold: **vasoconstriction**, shivering and hair erection.
- **Blood glucose** (control centre: pancreas). High glucose: **beta cells** release **insulin**; cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as **glycogen**. Low glucose: **alpha cells** release **glucagon**; the liver breaks glycogen down into glucose. Insulin and glucagon are **antagonistic**.
- **Water balance** (**osmoregulation**): when blood is too concentrated, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger the posterior pituitary to release more **ADH**. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water (by inserting **aquaporins**), so more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is made.

### When homeostasis fails

- Disorders happen when one part of the stimulus–response pathway breaks: the gland makes too little hormone (**hyposecretion**) or too much (**hypersecretion**), or the target cells stop responding.
- **Type 1 diabetes**: an **autoimmune** disease that destroys beta cells, so little or no insulin is made. Blood glucose stays high (**hyperglycaemia**), and glucose appears in the urine; people feel thirsty and lose weight. It is treated with insulin.
- **Type 2 diabetes** is different: insulin is made but target cells respond poorly (**insulin resistance**).
- **Hyperthyroidism**, often caused by **Graves' disease**: antibodies bind TSH receptors and switch the thyroid on outside negative feedback control. Thyroxine is high, TSH is low, metabolic rate is high (weight loss, heat intolerance, fast heart rate), and a **goitre** may form.
- **Diabetes insipidus**: too little ADH, or kidneys that do not respond, causing large volumes of dilute urine and thirst.

## Area of Study 3: How do scientific investigations develop understanding?

- Begin with a focused, testable question and a **hypothesis** with a reason: "If… then… because…".
- **Independent variable** (changed), **dependent variable** (measured), **controlled variables** (kept the same). Include a **control** group for comparison.
- Use **replicates** and calculate means, which reduces the effect of **random error**.
- **Random error** scatters results unpredictably; **systematic error** shifts all results the same way (for example an uncalibrated balance).
- **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value; **precision** is closeness of repeated results to each other; **validity** is whether the experiment really tests what it claims to.
- Consider safety and ethics, including **informed consent** for human participants and animal welfare.
- In the discussion: describe the trend, explain it with biology, state whether the hypothesis is supported, evaluate errors and limitations, and suggest specific improvements.

## Tips to remember

- **"All Cells Come from Cells"** — the three ideas of cell theory: All living things are made of cells, Cells are the basic unit, Cells come from existing cells.
- **"Pro = no"** — prokaryotes have *no* nucleus and *no* membrane-bound organelles. "Eu" means true: eukaryotes have a true nucleus.
- **SA:V shortcut** — for a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side. Double the side, halve the ratio. Picture a big ice block melting slower than crushed ice: small pieces have more surface for their size.
- **The protein factory** — picture a factory: the nucleus is the head office with the blueprints, ribosomes are workers, rough ER is the assembly line, the Golgi is the packing and shipping room, vesicles are delivery trucks, and mitochondria are the power station.
- **Osmosis rule: "Water follows salt"** (or any solute). Water always moves towards the side with more dissolved stuff. Hypo = "low" outside, so water goes in and the cell gets hippo-sized.
- **Active transport is "uphill"** — passive processes roll downhill on their own; going uphill against a gradient costs ATP.
- **"PMAT"** — Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase. Metaphase = **M**iddle; Anaphase = **A**part (or Away).
- **Interphase "Grow, Synthesise, Grow"** — G1, S, G2. DNA is copied in S for **S**ynthesis.
- **Cancer: accelerator and brakes** — oncogenes are an accelerator stuck down; faulty tumour suppressor genes are brakes that no longer work.
- **Potency: "Tom Plays Many Units"** (a made-up memory trick) — Totipotent, Pluripotent, Multipotent, Unipotent, from most to least flexible.
- **Xylem up, phloem flows** — "**X**ylem carries water up; **ph**loem carries **ph**ood (food) both ways." Xylem is dead; phloem is alive and needs ATP.
- **Transpiration on washing day** — the conditions that dry washing fastest (hot, dry, windy, sunny) are the same ones that speed up transpiration.
- **"Insulin puts glucose IN storage"**; **glucagon** sounds like "glucose gone", so it is released when glucose is gone and brings it back. **Beta cells** make insulin: "B for Bring it down".
- **ADH = "Add Water Back"** — more ADH means more water reabsorbed and less, darker urine.
- **Stimulus–response chain: "Silly Rabbits Can Eat Radishes"** (a made-up memory trick) — Stimulus, Receptor, Control centre, Effector, Response.
- **Negative feedback is a thermostat** — it switches the heater on when it is cold and off once the room is warm again.
- **Accuracy vs precision dartboard** — darts clustered together far from the bullseye are precise but not accurate (a sign of systematic error).

## Summary

- Cells are the basic unit of life; prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and SA:V limits how big any cell can get.
- Organelles divide the work of eukaryotic cells, and materials cross the fluid mosaic membrane by diffusion, osmosis, active transport and bulk transport.
- The cell cycle (interphase, mitosis, cytokinesis) is controlled by checkpoints and apoptosis; cancer results when mutations remove that control.
- Stem cells differ in potency, from totipotent to unipotent, and embryonic, adult and iPS cells each have benefits and drawbacks.
- Plants move water up the xylem by transpiration and cohesion–tension and sugars through the phloem by translocation; animal digestive, endocrine and excretory systems work together.
- Homeostasis uses the stimulus–response model and negative feedback to control temperature, blood glucose and water; disorders such as type 1 diabetes and Graves' disease arise when part of the pathway fails.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in every living cell, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic?
questions.explanation: All cells need to make proteins, so all have ribosomes. A nucleus (A) is tempting, but prokaryotes do not have one; their DNA sits in the nucleoid. Animal cells have no cell wall, and prokaryotes have no mitochondria.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped cell grows so that its side length doubles. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side halves the ratio. One quarter (D) is tempting because surface area rises four times, but volume rises eight times, so the ratio changes by 4 ÷ 8 = one half.

questions.prompt: A pancreatic cell makes and exports large amounts of digestive enzymes. Which organelles would you expect to be especially plentiful in this cell?
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins. They are made on ribosomes of the rough ER, then modified and packaged for export by the Golgi. Smooth ER (A) is tempting, but it makes lipids, not proteins, and lysosomes digest material rather than export it.

questions.prompt: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens to it?

options.B: It stays the same because no solute can cross
options.D: It swells and may burst as water enters

questions.explanation: Distilled water is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves in by osmosis towards the higher solute concentration. With no cell wall, the cell swells and can burst. Plasmolysis (C) only happens to plant cells in a hypertonic solution.

questions.prompt: Glucose moves into a cell through a carrier protein, down its concentration gradient, without using ATP. This is:
questions.explanation: Movement down a gradient through a protein, with no ATP, is facilitated diffusion. Active transport (B) also uses carrier proteins, which makes it tempting, but it moves substances against a gradient and needs ATP.

questions.prompt: In which stage of mitosis are sister chromatids pulled apart to opposite poles of the cell?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart ('A' for apart). In metaphase (B) the chromosomes line up in the middle but have not yet separated.

questions.prompt: Stem cells taken from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst can become any cell of the body but not the placenta. They are best described as:
questions.explanation: Pluripotent cells can form any body cell but not supporting tissues such as the placenta. Totipotent (A) is tempting because these cells are very flexible, but only the zygote and very early cells can form the placenta as well.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains how water rises to the top of a tall tree?

options.A: Living xylem cells actively pump water upward using ATP
options.B: Phloem carries water upward by translocation
options.C: Transpiration pulls a continuous column of water held together by cohesion and adhesion
options.D: Root pressure alone pushes water to the top

questions.explanation: The cohesion–tension model explains the movement: evaporation from leaves pulls on the water column, cohesion keeps it unbroken and adhesion helps it cling to xylem walls. Option A is a common misconception: mature xylem cells are dead, and no ATP is used.

questions.prompt: A runner becomes dehydrated during a long race. Which response is expected?

options.A: Less ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
options.B: More glucagon is released and the kidneys stop filtering
options.C: Less ADH is released and the collecting ducts become more permeable
options.D: More ADH is released, collecting ducts reabsorb more water and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced

questions.explanation: Dehydration makes the blood more concentrated, so the hypothalamus triggers more ADH release. ADH inserts aquaporins into collecting duct cells, so more water is reabsorbed. Option A is the response to drinking too much water, not to dehydration.

questions.prompt: Shortly after a meal, blood glucose rises. Which response restores the set point?

options.A: Alpha cells release glucagon and the liver breaks down glycogen
options.B: Beta cells release insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
options.D: Beta cells release glucagon and body cells take up glucose

questions.explanation: High glucose stimulates beta cells to release insulin, which increases glucose uptake and storage as glycogen. Option A describes the response to low glucose. Option D wrongly pairs beta cells with glucagon.

questions.prompt: What is the underlying cause of type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Target cells respond poorly to insulin
options.B: The pancreas makes too much glucagon
options.C: The immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells
options.D: The kidneys fail to reabsorb glucose

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune: beta cells are destroyed, so little or no insulin is made. Option A describes insulin resistance, the main feature of type 2 diabetes, which is why it is the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A student investigates how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed by counting oxygen bubbles. What is the dependent variable?

options.A: Number of bubbles produced per minute

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured: the bubble rate. Light intensity (B) is the independent variable, the factor deliberately changed. Temperature and plant type should be controlled variables.
